This TOMTOM has many more features than I'm use to but has the same basic functionality as pretty much any other GPS. The difference is in where you find that information. The reason I have mixed feelings is because this TOMTOM is so different from the 11-month old Magellan GPS I have. Also, there are a few features that just annoy me. For instance, with my Magellan I can press one button to find the route in text format. With the TOMTOM you have to make three selections to see the same thing - press once on the street name, then press once on the details button, then press the "browse as text option," and now you see the route in text format. Then when you want to get back to the map, you press done twice. To me this is very frustrating because when I'm navigating, I like to bounce back and forth between the map and the written route. However, I did not rate this GPS lower because of this since it's only my personal preference.

From a feature and option perspective, this GPS has a lot to offer. There are many points of interests (POIs), although the POIs are set up much differently than on my Magellan. There are HELP instructions on what to do if your car breaks down and what the rules of the road are for different states. In addition to the these features, you can edit your own maps, you can zoom in on them, you find the gas stations with the cheapest fuel prices (providing you subscribe to the TOMTOM daily fuel price updates), etc., etc. The reason I rated this TOMTOM three stars is because it offers too many selections making the system more complex than necessary, the screen is not as crisp as other GPS's I've seen, and some of the basic menu options are not as intuitive or as easy to get to as they are on the Magellan.

Update as of 12/05/09: I had my boyfriend try the GPS and he quickly became frustrated with the menu items and felt it was too complex. Although he was originally going to rate this TOMTOM 2 stars; he now agrees with my rating of 3 after he was shown some features. However, I had his 20-year old daughter try it and she loves the GPS and all the features it offers. For instance, she liked the ability to change the arrow into a car as you follow the GPS map and all the data that is displayed on the screen. She rates the GPS 4 stars only because the menus are sometimes a bit difficult to navigate. So it seems the younger generation might like this more than the older generation who usually don't prefer all the bells and whistles.

A Harmony user and works with a mac. Let me start by saying that my first universal remote was the Marantz RC2000. This thing was called the "Remote of the Gods" by Home Theater Magazine". This device could control all of my components and came with 4 macro buttons, which allowed me to turn on my TV then my cable box and then set the controls on the remote for that cable box. It was a great remote but not very "Wife" friendly. It was big, heavy and chewed through AA batteries.

That was then this is now. I just replaced my aging Logitech Harmony 880 (with failing button contacts) with the Logitech 900. The 880 was a fantastic leap forward with an activity "macro" based remote that walked you through the setup. The reason I know that the Harmony 880 was good was that once it was setup I never though about it again. It just worked.

The Logitech Harmony 900 builds on its predecessors. Unfortunately, you have to create a new account when setting up the Harmony 900. It cannot pick up your settings from an older Harmony remote. No a huge deal but if you haven't looked at the model numbers on your equipment in a few years this can be a bit of a pain. To ease that pain you should probably login to your original Harmony account and right down the make and model #s of all your equipment.

Initial setup was a bit different than the Harmony 880. No I should let you know that I setup the remote on Mac running OS X 10.6 (Snow Leopard). When connecting a Harmony 880 it gets detected and just works. The Harmony 900 gets detected as 2 devices. The first is the remote and the second is a network device. This surprised me at first but probably has something to do with the way the remote communicates with the RF receiver. Once you create your account and connect the unit it will download and update it's firmware. This will take a few minutes and then the remote will reboot.

It will then ask you to start listing your devices. In my case it was 7 (TV, DVD Player, TiVo Series 3, A/V Receiver, XBOX 360, a lighting controller and a Playstation 3. A special note about using a Playstation 3, the PS3 uses Bluetooth for its controllers and remote. It does not support Infrared. Logitech does sell an IR to Bluetooth transmitter for around $50. If you want to save some money pick up Nyko's Bluewave IR Dongle and Remote (for about $15). If you have the Bluewave don't add the Playstation 3 as a device, just add the Nyko Bluewave and system will understand that you have a PS3.

The setup was relatively painless. I had to manually setup the Lutron lighting controller. No when I say "manually" I don't mean that I had to have the Harmony 900 learn the commands. Logitech had the codes in its database. I mean that I had to go into the activities and add the "Lights On" and "Lights Off" to the Soft Buttons section.

The build quality of the 900 remote seems to be better than the 880. It has a sturdier feel with a rubber bottom for better grip. The screen and graphics are at a higher resolution and there is a nice bit of sliding animation when moving between pages. The remote fits in the charging cradle quite snugly with little room to miss the contacts (unlike early versions of the 880 charger).

I don't have any equipment at the moment that needs the RF portion of this remote so I can't comment on it. I'm sure there are several written and video reviews that cover this.

Over all I would recommend this remote for people who are somewhat technical. For people who have many components (and don't want to spend thousands on a Crestron controller) this is a must have.

Easy point and shoot, with easy to use menu. Please note that this camera does not shoot in HIGH DEFINITION.

The idea of migrating the storage of camcorder shots to an internal memory was very appealing with this camera. It stores up 16GB and there is a slot to add an SD card. Hence, there is no extra cost in buying an SD card, which is not the case for all camcorders in the same price range.

What we liked about the camcorder
- very light, very easy to hold and shoot.
- has a built in lense cap, which is terrific and mades the whole design have a much cleaner finish. Also, when you switch the camcorder on, it will tell you when you have not opened the lense cap!
- built in 16GB of ram and a slot to add an SD card
- a visible botton on the outside that allows you to choose between using the a) camcorder b) camera c) watch the movies stored
- the menu is very user friendly and some of the options we liked include:
i) grids to help you frame your shot
ii) focus that allows for auto focusing, face recognition or manual focusing
iii) simpe scence shot options: sports or portraits
IV) has anti shake option, which comes in handy if you are using the zoom (also see below for the not so great bits about the zoom).
vi) up load to utube is very easy
v) cuts on wind noise (it works and reduces the muffle sound)
vii) the program for editing your shot is very simple, as the intention is to allow you to edit (if any) before loading to utube or send it for friends/family to see. If you are looking for a more sophicated finish then you need to buy a separate program.

Maybe it is the price bracket this camcorder falls within, but we would have liked to see improvements in the following:

- the zoom feature is great to a point, but if you plan to use it to its full capacity then I would recommend that you use a tripod. Otherwise, the whole shot comes out very 'shakened'.
- we noticed that the zoom button was more sensitive compared with other camcorders in the same price range, which made it very difficult to zoom in and out without you feeling that you were travelling through the stargate!
- the camcorder and camera options are best used in good lighting. Not advisable for low lighting events.
- no flash light.

A Fantastic, Well thought out Tripod. I have three main uses for tripods, food photography, nature photography and to hold up a spotting scope. This tripod succeeds wonderfully at two of those. It is great for nature photography and supporting the spotting scope. I am 6' 3" and I love that height of this tripod. even without extending the center post, I can comfortably use the tripod when standing.

This is a fantastic birdwatching tripod for my spotting scope. The carbon fiber material is light and rugid. Vanguard has remembered the little things, for example, the upper legs are padded which is huge in when trying to spot an owl in Minnesota at twenty below. The insulation makes the tripod much more comfortable to handle, equally when shooting images of Northern lights.

The legs are fairly sturdy although I feel that here is a little more play in the carbon fiber over my older aluminum, Bogen tripod. I was a little disappointed that there are just a few angle settings for the legs. They click into 30 and about 60 degrees. It would be nice to have more granular settings, so I find myself altering leg lengths more than my other tripod. The feet are well designed with hard steel spikes with nice rubber feet for indoor uses. Both options allow for good stable footings.

Also there are some great other details like leveling bubbles on the top of the tripod and ball head. Also, I like that they though to include a hook at the bottom of the center post for adding stability weights. The leg releases are easy to use and have held tight during all my time in the field with the tripod.

Where I wish they had put more into this tripod is the ball head. It doesn't seem to live up to the tripod body. I miss a pan handle and while I appreciate the feel and functionality of the locking knobs, it just seems like it is not the pro quality of the rest of the tripod. There is a second leveling bubble on the head itself which is fantastic. But probably the biggest drawback is the quick release plate. It is not quick at all, it requires quite a bit of screwing with thumbscrew to attach. Also there is not set screw on the "quick" release plate.

Pros
+ Height
+ padded legs for comfort in cold weather
+ Light Weight
+ Great feet, both the grippy robber shoes and the steel spikes
+ built in leveling bubbles
+ Functional and strong leg locks
+ built in hook on bottom of center post
+ Second leveling bubble on the head

Cons
- No built in strap
- Carrying case is ok (this is more a neutral than a con)
- the head is not great
- limited leg angles
- Head could be better
- Somewhat awkward and slow quick release plates
- Lacks a panning arm.

In General, this is an awesome tripod, but for the money I would have expected a little more, especially a strap and a better head unit. But I have to admit I love this tripod. I would have put 4.5 stars if possible, but for $500 my expectation for a "Professional" tripod head is a little higher. But for my uses it's awesome, it holds the Spotting Scope will but again, lack of a panning arm hinders it. From the shoulders down, the best I've seen.

Otherwise the functionality is pretty much the same, right down to the less than intuitive menus and lack of an easy way to simply input a coordinate. If you are trying to set a waypoint or mark a location, it is very straight forward. Likewise, downloading geocache coordinates is great. However, I have yet to find a great way to input a coordinate. Why isn't there an option of a "Go to this coordinate" button that then prompts you to enter the coordinate? That seems completely intuitive to me, yet I cannot find this functionality on either this or the etrex. (please comment if you know how to do this, I have just been altering existing waypoints or caches.)

I don't think I could be happier with the form factor. It fits well in the hand and is, for lack of a better word, cute. I have had fun using this with the boys and I appreciate another excuse to get them outside and almost unwired for a while. Decent headphones biggest drawback is distortion at moderately high volumes. I'm pretty happy with these headphones, I received a reviewer pair intending to use them as my work headphones, and hope to make use of the sound canceling capabilities. My previous head phones are [[ASIN:B002YOENAS Sennheiser PXC 310 BT Compact Noise-Canceling Travel Headphones with Bluetooth Technology (Black)]] so that is what I am comparing them to.

Sound---

I am very happy with the clarity of the sound from these headphones. The music is crisp and has decent highs and lows. The one thing I am a little disappointed with is there seems to be a lot of distortion when turned to just a moderately high volume. Which probably works well with my use at work, but I can't truly crank these headphones without getting too much distortion. Of course this is probably good for my hearing, but to continue the comparison to the Sennheisers, these have less capability at higher volumes.

When listening to these at lower volume though, they are very nice. I'm not a huge audiophile, but I can appreciate the sound quality these deliver.

Sound canceling appears to work fairly well. I can at least attest to the fact that I missed phone calls while listening to these, I am interested to see how the will work to cut airplane noise.

Design ---

I'm impressed with the way these headphones have been designed to fold for storage and transport. They are not as compact as my Sennheisers, but they do fold into a decent size and the nice leatherette case holds them well, with space to spare for extra accessories. The ear pieces swivel well to form to you head, the cable connects firmly and securely, and the battery compartment is well designed.

Also, I am impressed that they thought to add an adapter for an airline headphone jack. I am looking forward to having these to listen to on my next air trip.

Comfort---

The ear pieces are nicely padded that make a nice comfortable fit. I have historically only used ear buds so at times my ears seem to get warm due to the coverage of the ear pieces. The bar is padded but noticeable on your head, again for those used to earbuds this takes an adjustment.

Summary---

All in all these are nice headphones. I prefer my Sennheisers which do deliver a little better sound on the corded connection (less sound quality over Bluetooth.) However, I am happy with these, but not enough to justify the price savings over the Sennheisers.

Universal Router extender - however it won't help in a motel/hotel. My first question was "What is 802.11ac?" - In December 2011 "802.11ac" was the next evolution of WiFi & enabled wireless speeds over a gigabit per second.

"b" was the first there was (802.11b) which provided up to 11 mbps data rates per radio in the 2.4 GHz spectrum.
"a" was the next evolution (802.11a) which provided up to 54 mbps data rates per radio in the 5 GHz spectrum.
"g"came out shortly after enabling 54 mbps per radio in the 2.4 GHz spectrum.
"n" was ratified in 2009 (802.11n) allows for data rates up to 600 mbps per radio.
"ac" builds on 802.11n.

This one fits in my pocket and costs less than $20. Times have changed.

This device connects to my PC with a USB Type A connector but at 3.0 speeds, meaning I can transfer plenty of data quickly without waiting half the day for it all to transfer. This is handy for moving picture archives or movie files which tend to be large. Both my Windows and my Linux systems see this device and are able to communicate with it.

The other interface to this device is a MicroUSB connector, which works for older Android phones. Newer phones have a USB-C connector so be sure that your phone can use this device if that is your intended purpose. It comes with an app for installing on your Android phone to make it easier to manage. I don't have an Android phone anymore but I do have a tablet that runs Android, and this device connects to it without issue.

It is small enough that it can fit in the coin pocket of my jeans with plenty of room to spare. This is both good and bad. On one hand, it is very easy to find room for this device no matter how burdened and heavily packed you are but it also means it is easy to misplace. I'd suggest adding a lanyard.

So far I am pleased with this device. It is reliable, it has plenty of storage and it works with my PC as well as Android phones. It would be more useful with a lanyard and a USB-C option would be welcome, even if sold as a separate product entirely.

Decent Slider, but Room for Improvement. I am primarily a stills shooter. That said, I do have an excellent camera that is very capable of shooting video and I do need it for such on occasion. I was interested in this camera slider as a way to get smooth shots and to reduce reliance on lens-based stabilization which is not included in my camera body. This has been a learning experience and while I like this slider there is definitely room for improvement.

I will start with the basics. This is a large and fairly heavy animal, which is to be expected. It is roughly 3' long and in it’s most basic configuration rests on a flat surface with no issues. It does have some adjustments that can be made to the individual feet on the frame so it can be adjusted slightly for uneven but mostly level surfaces without using any other equipment. To get much more versatility out of it, though, it can be mounted on tripods on either end to raise it higher or to set up angular shots.

The motor on the frame is controlled by a remote which comes with a battery pack. The remote is not wireless and has to be connected to the motor via the provided cabling. This is all right, but wireless functionality would make it much more versatile. It should be noted that the remote controls the slider, not the camera. I had some concern about this in the very beginning, thinking that the remote would be incompatible with my camera and that this unit would not work for me.

I encountered some issues that bother me. First, when powered on and running the motor runs the slider down the track until it is either stopped or a stop point is set. If one is not set, it bumps into the end and keeps trying to go beyond, making an awful noise that will surely mess up any video that requires sound. In my mind, the motor should detect when it hits the end and stop, even if start and stop points are not set.

When the motor is running and it is not near a stop point, it runs at constant speed and it is very smooth. When manually paused, it stops quickly but it doesn’t jerk to an abrupt stop like it hit something. But, if one of the end points are set and is reached, the motor slows down, then jerks to a stop, enough to notice in video footage. This is most obvious when the remote is set up to film in a loop as the issue can be observed repeatedly.

The motor is not silent, though it is quiet. It is not loud enough to ruin a shot unless absolute quiet is needed, and the motor produces a low-volume, low-frequency hum that slightly resembles the sound of an electric trolling motor on a bass boat, but quieter. The point is that it is by no means silent, but it should be good enough in the majority of cases. This is out the window if the motor is allowed to reach the end of the track before it is stopped, in which case the noise is likely to be a serious issue.

This is a decent slider and if used with some thought will serve nicely. There are definitely some places where it could be improved, particularly in the way it fails to handle reaching the end of tracks.

Works Very Well for Us; Easy to Understand and Operate. UPDATE - Failed after under two weeks. UPDATE 05/15/2021 - It lasted less than two weeks and it died. During playback the player freezes on discs known to be good, and in order to get6 the player to respond I have to disconnect the power from it. It was great while it lasted, I guess.

Original review follows.

===

I have wanted a Blu-Ray player for a while and I have had reason to suspect that my DVD player is dying. I have a flat-screen Sony television so I figured this player would connect and work with it without too much effort. I was right and it has worked very well for my family and me.

This is a straightforward device. I connected it to the TV via the provided HDMI cable, selected that input and immediately was able to get signal from it. I popped in a disc and it loaded up to the menu. That’s exactly what I expected to happen. In operation using the remote it has worked very much like my old DVD player – remote is laid out a bit differently but the operation is the same and it provides buttons to stop, fast forward and reverse, pause, eject, select the root menu and more. The remote had given us no issues so far, though it does need to have near line-of-site with the player in order for the player to see it and respond.

The footprint is much smaller than my older DVD player and required a bit of rearrangement in my entertainment center. The whole unit is smaller than a ream of paper and weighs next to nothing.

It has built-in WiFi and makes it easy to access online streaming services. However, I will confess that I haven’t yet tried this as I try to keep my WiFi device list small. I will experiment with this when there is time.

So far we have seen no issues with playback – no skips or stutters or freezes. I have a couple of discs that I know to cause issues for my DVD player that I will try in this player and see if it fares better, though I believe the discs are actually bad.

So far I have had a positive experience with this player and based on that I am happy to recommend it. It seems to work well and it is easy to understand and operate. It isn’t particularly expensive either which is a big plus.

Inexpensive Macro Filter Set. I selected these macro filters to go with a 77mm Fujinon lens. I have used these types of filters with an older camera and wanted a set for my new camera, and after researching available options I chose these. These are decent macro filters though there is some room for improvement.

These are about as basic as it gets. They’re not fancy, they’re just screw-on filters designed to fit lenses with a 77mm thread. They fit my lens just fine and I have had no trouble removing them when I am done. These are straight glass and with the exception of the +10 filter there is little distortion. The +10 filter has a lot of edge distortion but clarity in the middle, which is very much like other sets like these I have used.

There is a problem with the +1 filter in my set. The glass is loose in the ring and it actually rattles when I handle it. It doesn’t seem to be loose enough to come out of the ring. It does concern me that it could come out, though. I would be more concerned about this if I used this particular filter more, but that’s not the point.

This is not a bad set, but the quality is not as good as it should be. The filters work well enough, but I am concerned that the glass might separate from the ring, based on one of them in my set. So far it hasn’t happened.

Keyboard Slipped Past the QC Department. For the most part I have had good fortune with Logitech peripherals. As I write this I am using an MX Ergo trackball which is the best mouse/trackball I have ever used. I looked to the MK470 mouse/keyboard combination with the idea of using it with a laptop running Linux. I had high expectations for the keyboard but lower expectations for the mouse due to the size and shape. Both failed me, but in completely different ways.

I will start with this: this combo does not use a unifying receiver so if you want to use another peripheral with this combo you’ll need either another USB port or connect via Bluetooth. That’s all right as long as you recognize that up front. It’s a mild disappointment, but it was clear up front so this was not a surprise.

The mouse and the keyboard both have the batteries installed already. The keyboard takes 2 AAA batteries and the mouse takes one AA battery. I question the logic behind using different battery sizes.

I plugged the receiver into my laptop running Linux with the latest kernel, and both peripherals were immediately usable. That’s a plus.

The first problem I have is with the mouse. The mouse works just fine but is such a low-profile device that it is uncomfortable for me to use. I have a travel mouse that actually fits my hand a little better and that says a lot. For someone with very small hands this one will serve acceptably as a basic two-button travel mouse. To be fair, I knew this ahead of time so I cannot complain too much. It does work correctly and in a pinch I can work with it.

The keyboard is a completely different matter entirely. It works just fine – except for the “P” key. For that specific key, I have to bear down very hard to get it to register at all. I tried leaning the keyboard on its side and tapping it gently in case something was caught in the switch and I have tried my best to clean it without disassembly. No matter what I have tried, the “P” key continues to be insensitive to the point of rendering the keyboard unusable.

I really wanted to like this keyboard, and I knew the mouse would be small. Unfortunately, because the keyboard I received doesn’t work properly I can’t use it and can’t rate it favorably. It’s a shame – I imagine I got a bad unit (it happens), but I cannot recommend a product based on an assumption.

UPDATE 10/31/2019:

I popped off the "P" key and looked at the mechanism underneath, since the keyboard was not otherwise useful. It does not appear to be broken, damaged or obstructed in any way. For this particular key, the plastic key cover needs a small bead in the center underneath to push down the silicone membrane to make contact. Using a very small piece of tape and a tiny ball (about the size of a pin head) I was able to add such to the key cover to get it working without damaging any parts, without changing the feel while typing, and without spending any money. However, this should not have been necessary as this should have been tested properly before pack-and-ship; my review and rating stand.

Works Well for Me. Of the three main GPS receiver manufacturers - Garmin, TomTom and Magellan - I have had the most success with TomTom devices. My first GPS was a TomTom and it served me well for years until the map outgrew the memory. I was excited to have the opportunity to try this one; so far, it has been a good unit, though I do not care for the menu system.

This is a larger unit than the original one I had, upgrading from a 4.3" to a 6". I like the screen real estate. For all that screen space, TomTom has made good use of it, maximizing the visible map and keeping the interface clean and uncluttered. One area where I am slightly disappointed, though, is in the speed display which is a little small - it's good to keep it out of the way but it's a little smaller than I like and it a bit harder to read. If you use your GPS for watching your speed, this could be a problem.

Navigation is easy. I like the way this unit routes me to my destination yet does not nag me when I go off the chosen route. Others I have used (including my old TomTom) would badger me to make a U-turn for a while before deciding that there was another way to get where I was going. This unit does make that point sometimes, but it also is smart enough to reroute when I have multiple similar routes.

The biggest plus for this unit (and it seems to be a TomTom thing) is that the voice very clearly enunciates without distortion or the unit buzzing. I have had this issue with every other unit of every other brand, but my old TomTom was clear and understandible even at higher volumes. Since this one is the same, I believe TomTom has a better understanding of how to build a unit that sounds right.

Navigating from work to home is usually a straight shot down the interstate for 40+ miles and a little bit of backroads. To test, I instead took a long, out-of-the-way route that I use when there is heavy traffic volume. Knowing it would try to put me on the interstate, I set the farthest point as a first leg, then set it to take me home from there. The route it chose was actually only slightly different than the one I had chosen already, and the difference was that I accounted for rush hour traffic.

Speaking of traffic... This unit gathers traffic data without relying on mobile data. I greatly prefer this to having to run an app on my phone and letting it gather traffic info from online. So far I have not had it report a reroute due to traffic; I will come back here and update when it does.

The main complaint I have about this GPS is the menu system. WIth TomTom's older units, the menu system was fairly traditional and was smiliar to that of a PC application menu system (sorta). The new interface has a scrolling row of icons that lead to more icons. I am not a fan of this type of interface and is the one thing I would change about this unit if I could.

When this unit is first powered on and set up it downloads a hefty amount of data to update the map. This is unavoidable, unfortunately. Do not be discouraged by this - it will be up to date and ready to go when it finishes.

I have not had any real issues with this unit so far. It works well and I like how it navigates. I don't like the menu system and find it very awkward, but it gets me where I want to go with little fuss.

Decent Unpowered USB Hub. One of the problems I have seen with the latest crop of notebooks and Ultrabooks that have come out is a lack of USB ports. There's usually a need for more ports than these systems have and it gets frustrating. A small USB hub like this is a good solution. That said, this particular hub does not have a separate power source so some consideration must be made when plugging in power-hungry devices.

From a design stantpoint this is a solid unit, shaped to be accessible without being huge. It has a little weight to it and this is helpful for keeping it stable. The addition of Velcro strips in the package to secure it in one place is a welcome inclusion and makes securing the hub very simple no matter what your configuration is.

The hub provides four USB 3.1 type A ports. Let me state what should be obvious - this will not convert a USB 1.1 or 2.0 port into a 3.1 port, so plug it into a 3.1 port if you want the speed across the hub. For my specific uses, it does not need to be a high-speed hub and I am find with using it as a 2.0 hub, but admittedly that's slightly wasteful.

There is no power port on this hub and there is no DC adapter in the box. So, any power that the hub needs comes through the onboard port into which it is plugged. That's fine for low-power devices like mice, keyboards, memory sticks and so on, but if the intent is to plug in such things as USB hard drives with no external power supply this can cause some headaches. No, one drive isn't going to overload the hub, but if you have multiple drives attached there may be reliability issues when they starve one another for power. When the device plugged in has its own power supply (like a big backup drive), this has little impact on the hub.

The point is, plan carefully how you intend to use the hub.

I like this hub and it does a good job for what it is. It has given me three extra ports on an Ultrabook I use which is all I could ask for. The ability to power this hub with it's own power supply would be the only area for improvement I could find.

Bluetooth Connectivity a Big Plus; Pen is Mediocre at Best. NOTE: This review is written for the Small, Bluetooth edition.

I have been using Wacom Intuos and Bamboo tablets for years, not really for graphic arts but more for digital handwriting and for use as an alternative to traditional mice and trackballs. My present solution is an Intuos 5 medium which seems to be about the right fit for my hands and my work space. The one drawback has been that it’s a wired solution. This new Intuos is a Bluetooth solution and it is definitely a step forward. For me the challenge is downgrading to the small from the medium, but it’s a good fit for me when traveling and when working in cluttered spaces.

To approximate the size, it is roughly equivalent to 7” tablet in size. It’s small enough to tuck away in a corner of a desk when not in use, and when it is being used it does not take up large amounts of real estate. The design itself makes it suitable for use just about anywhere it can be set down and kept stable - one of the reasons I like drawing tablets more than traditional mice.

The Bluetooth connectivity is new to me, and I was pleasantly surprised to find that this unit can connect via USB as well. So, if your system is like one of mine and the Bluetooth doesn’t work, this drawing tablet still will work.

I have it connected to my Windows 10 system. I have not yet made the effort to get it working with my Linux system, though I expect there will be some labor involved to make that work. I’ll revisit that later.

In operation, this is a straightforward drawing tablet though it is an improvement over my Intuos 5 in some ways. Of course the Bluetooth is a step up, but I was surprised by the increased number of pressure levels which is effectively doubled over my old tablet - 4096 vs 2048. For someone like me, this is not a huge difference and I don’t take advantage, but for someone who is very serious about fine digital artwork this can be a huge benefit. For use in handwriting, it is not especially important as even 512 pressure levels (like my original Bamboo small) is more than sufficient.

When you register, you get a choice between three Corel titles, of which you can select two (for the medium you get all three). Some may find the choice difficult - Painter Essentials 6, AfterShot 6 and Clip Studio Paint Pro (2 years) - but for me, having AfterShot is more than enough.

There is a downside to this little tablet, though - the pen is mediocre. There is no comfort grip, changing the nib is a pain, and there’s a very limited number of replacement nibs for it. It’s the one weak spot in an otherwise nice product, and even then it’s not all that bad.

The hardest part for me with this specific tablet is the move from a medium to a small, but this this counterbalanced by the Bluetooth connectivity and the inclusion of the Corel titles, specifically AfterShot. This is a very nice drawing solution and is it priced nicely. I’d recommend the small for anyone either just getting started or experimenting; the medium is a better fit for those more experienced or needing more real estate. I would choose a different pen if available, though.

Flat Midrange. I will start by saying that I am typically not a fan of ear buds. I will also say that the very best headphones I have is a set of Sony active noise canceling ear buds. I have always had good success with Sony audio products and I regard the brand as an upper mid-range line. These buds are disappointing in that, while they’re comfortable for ear buds, the sound profile is lacking, specifically in the midrange.

This is a basic set of ear buds that work as you might expect. They do not have ANC functionality, there is no battery or battery pack and there is no Bluetooth functionality. These are straight plug-in audio gear with no fancy features. These will work with just about any device that provides a 3.5mm audio jack.

Most ear buds are uncomfortable to me, but these are surprisingly comfortable and I can wear these for a good bit of time. They come with several inserts of varying sizes so you can find the size that fits your ear canal just right. The included inserts are soft and do not irritate my ears as much as others have done in the past. I still very much prefer over-the-ear headphones which is a personal preference more than anything.

So, where’s the problem? The problem lies in the sound profile which is unbalanced. Having used literally dozens of sets of ear buds and headphones over the past 3-5 years I have developed a good feel for what sounds right and what doesn’t. Most ear buds have one of two issues, either way too much bass or almost none at all. These are surprising in that they actually get the bass just about right, not too heavy and not too light. The highs are very bright and clear, perhaps a touch too piercing for my tastes but not to the point of being unacceptable. The midrange, though, is flat. The result is that music sounds somewhat sterile and lackluster. This is similar to the issue I have seen with my Bose headset. These still sound good, but they fall short of where they could and should be.

Normally I would rate ear buds with a glitch in the sound profile a little higher, as they’re still quite usable and they sound decent. But, these are much more expensive than the average and I have heard less expensive buds with more balanced sound. Sony makes a number of sets of ear buds and headphones, but these are not among their best offerings.

Decent After Some Initial Disappointment. Philips is a household name when it comes to electronics and this was my first opportunity to play with their camcorder/camera line. This camera was initially very disappointing but after giving it a second chance I have come to appreciate it more. I am completely revising this review.

This is an attractive little camera, wine red and compact. It is a little smaller than an ice cream sandwich, which makes it ideal for on-the-go imaging and also for people who dislike toting a heavier camera around. Because this camera is waterproof it feels ruggedized and solid, and the camera is able to withstand being dropped from low heights. Overall, it is a well-built product.

I plugged in the camera and I let it charge, and it took about an hour to fully charge. This was a pleasant surprise - other brands of cameras I have used take 2-4 hours so Philips has the charging mechanism down fairly well.

My first big disappointment happened when I set up for recording. By default, the camcorder is set for HD recording and it reported that I had about 15 seconds of recording. When I started recording, it stopped shortly thereafter. Sure enough, it ate up all the space available. It was at this point I realized that there was no MicroSD card in the package - not even a small one. I had to dig online to find the internal capacity of the camera - 128MB. A camcorder that cannot record even 1 minute of video is all but useless. This was evidence of simply cutting corners. Granted, I could set recording to standard resolution and I could get more video time but still not enough to be considered useful. Why Philips does not include more internal storage in this camera is completely beyond me.

My initial video tests were abyssmal. I tried several things to get the video quality up but I was unable to get things to look very good. Videos were grainy, pixelated and otherwise looked bad. I tried setting the recording mode (scene) manually and while that did help it did not improve the video quality enough to make a real difference. I moved the video to the computer and it looked even worse.

It occurred to me that all of my videos were shot in the evening with lower light. I decided to take a video of my cat in the middle of the day instead and the results were vastly better, to the point of actually looking quite good! So, I set the mode to "Auto" and recorded about 30 seconds worth of footage, copied the video to the computer and everything looked great. Apparently, the low-light capabilities of this camcorder are not great but it's daylight recording is very good.

The anti-shake capabilities on this camcorder are excellent. There seems to be a slight filming delay which allows the camcorder to compensate for slight motion - this is good for when you're outside and you have a shiver.

Still image quality is good when using good lighting but is average at best when in low-light conditions. With the small internal storage there is room for pictures but again this will fill up fairly quickly, especially at full resolution.

I had high hopes for this camcorder/camera and though I was initially very disappointed with it I have come to a point of satisfaction with it. It does not perform well in low light, even with the flash on, but in daylight it is very good. The storage capacity (or, rather, the lack thereof) really is inexcusable but for an on-the-go camera/camcorder it's worth a look. As long as this is not going to be a night-life camera, it's good.

Sound Clarity vs. QuietComfort 15: A comparative review. I recently acquired a pair of Able Planet Sound Clarity (SC hereafter) headphones, just 6 days after purchasing a pair of Bose Quiet Comfort 15 Noise Canceling headphones (QC15 hereafter). I got a very good deal on the Able Planet phones, which is the main reason I bought them. With both sets in hand, I have been able to do a side-by-side comparison between them. Bose is generally regarded as the Gold Standard when it comes to active noise canceling phones so this review is spun in that regard. I have not had a chance to try the Sennheiser offerings, so I cannot comment on those.

In summary, the Able Planet phones compare reasonably well against the Bose phones, but there are some trade-offs between the two. Which set to buy depends on the personal preferences and intended uses.

First off, the phones look very similar to one another. The general design is the same, with an over-the-ear design, soft pads and an on-off switch for noise cancellation. There are some very distinct differences, though, that are not obvious at a glance. First, the detachable cord plugs in somewhat differently, the SC having a jack that this flush with the phone and the QC15 having a jack that is inset within the base of the phone, with a molded plug. The battery compartment is also accessed differently, the SC having a sliding cover exposing 2 AAA batteries and the QC15 having a flip-up cover for a single AAA battery.

Another visible difference is in the cord that is included with the SC phones - it has a volume control thumb wheel. The QC15 phones have simply on/off. I like being able to adjust the volume without fiddling with the source such as a computer.

Comfort-wise, Bose has an upper hand on Able Planet. While both have an over-the-ear design which covers the ear, the SC cup is a hair smaller and as such it cannot cover the whole ear as easily as the QC15. That said, the SC phones are still comfortable and the difference is minor.

The noise canceling aspect of the SC phones is very good but it does not compare to the QC15 headset. Standing next to a running air handler that is roughly the size of a minivan, the SC is able to wipe out a good portion of the noise to make the level comfortable. The QC15 wiped out the sound of the air handler completely, to the point that it was difficult to tell if it was even turned on.

I was interested in the Linx Audio aspect of the SC phones and at first I was very disappointed. The high range is somewhat dampened, "S" sometimes sounding like "PH". However, the mid and low ranges are solid and are very rich, whereas Bose sounds good but has remarkably less depth. The QC15 phones are primarily noise canceling phones, and sound quality is secondary to that. The SC headset achieves a better balance of sound to noise canceling.

Once very distinct advantage that the SC headset has is that the phones will work without power, though noise canceling does not work in that case. The QC15 requires a working battery and must be turned on to work at all.

Right out of the box, my SC phones were defective. I contacted Able Planet, hoping I could get some advice on how to adjust them, but instead I got an RMA number. Less than 2 weeks later I had a new, working pair in my hands that work much better than the initial pair. Customer service at Able Planet is very responsive, professional and courteous. With the LIFETIME warranty on their headphones, Bose cannot answer with their 2-year warranty.

Which pair to buy is a matter of preference and intended use. If the intended primary use is noise cancellation and comfort, Bose is the right choice. For listening to music with the ability to engage noise canceling when needed, Able Planet is a better choice. Considering the 2-year Bose warranty against an Able Planet lifetime warranty, though, is hard to ignore.

As I use my phones for listening to music more than anything else, I use the Able Planet headset as my primary headset and I keep my Bose headset as a backup.

Very strong alternative in the GPS market. I purchased a Delorme PN-40 GPS for the purpose of geocaching. I already own a Garmin GPSMap 60CSx and a Garmin eTrex Legend, so although I did not really need another unit I wanted one so that when geocaching with my kids we would each be carrying a GPS and not reliant on one another. I have been very satisfied with my Garmin units but was impressed with the reviews and feature set of the Delorme, so I bought it with the expectation of it being acceptable for my uses as a backup unit. It has exceeded my expectations. It is not without flaws but it is a tremendous GPS that is very much worth every penny of the purchase price.

It is very similar in hard interface layout to my 60CSx, with the same buttons doing similar functions though in different locations. This makes working with the Delorme simple in that I immediately found myself familiar with how to work this GPS. The software interface is different, though, and is unlike any other unit with which I have worked. Different is not wrong, but it means a learning curve for those who use Garmin or Magellan units.

The first power-on of this unit is the most painful as it searches for the satellites. After this initial acquisition, however, power-up is always appreciably faster and the acquisition of satellites faster.

Once the GPS has acquired the satellites, it has proven itself to be very accurate and stable. It is not unusual to navigate to a location and have the unit lead me to a point less than a foot away from the lat/long specified. Reported accuracy on the screen is typically between 6 and 11 feet.

The accuracy does diminish under heavy canopy but no more so than my Garmins do. In dense tree cover I found that it maintains its location quite well most of the time, though it occasionally gets confused and leads me in circles. It seems to do this at times when my 60CSx is having no trouble, but it also seems to have no trouble when the Garmins are confused. This brings up a good point - different GPS manufacturers, using differing chip sets, will have varying environments in which their GPS units work better than others and sometimes not as well as others. It is important to keep this in mind and to select a unit that is best suited for the need.

The compass is excellent. Once calibrated it seems to be very accurate and does not need for the unit to be held level flat when in use in order to get a correct bearing. The 3D compass is something that is lacking in my Garmin units, but newer units have this feature now and it's wonderful. Manually calibrating the compass is easy and all you have to do is to follow the instructions on the screen (it equates to a series of arm motions).

This is a rugged and sturdy unit and can handle some jostling. It does as well in wet, rainy weather as it does on clear days. It is waterproof and can be submerged, but I am not daring enough to try this voluntarily.

One point on which many people complain is the screen size. Yes, it has a smaller screen than average units but it also seems to be bright and readable even in direct sunlight. Sure, larger would be nice but clear and readable is far preferable.

Delorme ships their Topo product with this GPS and it is the deal-maker that gives this GPS a decided edge. The maps may be cut and transferred to the PN-40 through Topo, or the pre-cut maps may be used instead. To get Garmin's MapSource costs an extra $100, which makes the PN-40 an even better deal. The maps are of good quality and are sufficient for hiking and driving alike. For most uses the pre-cup maps will be sufficient, but higher resolution images can be cut from Topo.

Right out of the box, my PN-40 was defective and had problem with the screen. I was not convinced that it was a problem until I called Delorme, and I was told to ship it back. In one week's time I had a completely new unit that has worked flawlessly ever since. While I was disappointed with the first unit being defective, I was shocked at how responsive Delorme is to customer requests for assistance. It is clear to me that they stand behind their product.

Less than three weeks after I purchased my PN-40, Delorme released Topo 8. My unit shipped with Topo 7. I called Delorme and asked about an upgrade, and for the cost of shipping a new Topo 8 DVD set was sent to me.

Map updates on the PN-40 are FAST. Scrolling is not exactly smooth but the dual-core processor embedded within keeps up quite admirably.

One drawback with this unit is that, at this time, importing waypoints and geocaches requires a different software set than can be used with Garmin and Magellan units. It can be done with Topo, and for geocachers there is Cache Register, but GSAK and other common tools do not transfer successfully at this time. Hopefully this will be remedied in the near future. Granted, this is easy enough to do, but one cannot have a single software application that can work with multiple units of different brand.

Another drawback is that this GPS loves batteries. On new, fully-charged NiMH batteries one can expect maybe 10 hours of operation before the unit gracefully turns itself off. On a long trek it is therefore a good idea to bring along extra batteries. Because alkalines tend to drain more quickly in electronics, I would recommend using either NiMH or lithium batteries.

The Delorme PN-40 is a very nice GPS for consumer use. It is accurate, it holds its signal well, has a great display and comes with Topo which combined all make this unit hard to pass up. It's not perfect by any means, but it is still excellent and should be considered when looking for a good handheld GPS.

So, with some trial and error, and a lot more time than I anticipated building the telescope, I finally got it assembled. Swell briefcase. Works fine with my 13" MBP.. Now that I'm transitioning to a more corporate world I figured it's about time I get a more "professional"-looking carrying satchel than my Osprey backpack. The only laptops I possess range around thirteen inches, as I find carrying anything heavier than that is far too large to be considered portable.

This briefcase has it all. There are pockets galore; at times I feel there are too many as I keep unzipping the wrong pocket or can't remember in which pocket I put something, so I wish the tags would've been different somehow. Maybe have some lanyards on some or another.

But inside the pockets you get even more pockets and sashes to separate compartments. The material is sturdy and has held up just fine in this insane Chicago spring weather. We've had temperatures ranging from 40-80 in just two weeks, as well as rainy and dry weathers. Chicago, I tell ya!
My 2010 13" MBP fits fine in the main laptop sleeve without sliding around much, and I'm not able to feel much wait on my shoulder from carrying it around all day, along with a couple of books, a Hobonichi planner, and my pencil case.

The main flaw I will say this has is the shoulder strap. It's not easily adjustable, and I still haven't fully figured it out. There is a buckle in the middle on either side--one static, and the other adjustable. But the adjustable buckle doesn't allow the strap easy give, and so I can't for the life of me get it to a comfortable length.
The removable strap is sturdy otherwise.

The other issue is the clasp holding the two handles together. It's not long enough, so instead of closing it with one hand I'm having to use both hands to squeeze the handles together before being able to snap the button together.

All in all, it's a great briefcase usable even with 13" laptops, but the shoulder strap and the handle clasp need better, user-friendly improvements.

Amazing IEMs with a couple of noticeable drawbacks.. I am not an audiophile by any means. I have Rockbox installed on my iPod video classic with a FiiO amp attached, all loaded with FLAC tunes. I listen to Spotify at work. That's the extent of my musical needs.
I have Audio-Technica headphones, and dream of some day owning custom Kaisers. That's my background.

I was pretty excited to get these. Right after ordering, I watched a few YouTube videos on them, and read up on Head-Fi. For the price, 1More seems to deliver outstanding products. Needless to say, I was pretty excited.

The box finally came and I was found to be very impressed with the presentation. You get a nice, magnetic box housing the IEMs, a leather(ette?) pouch, and multiple choices of ear piece tips. For starters, I found that the ear piece tips pre-attached to the IEMs were the most fitted for me, but I still do not find them perfect. They slide down a bit when in my ear, so there is some loss of sound. I will have to buy some aftermarket ones.

The microphone is also sub-par. This is the first time I've used a mic with headphones, and most of my calls could not catch my voice properly. I would get complaints that I sounded muffled or far away, and so I've resorted to using the phone mic most of the time. The mic buttons work flawlessly for playback features, however.

As for the sound, it's fantastic. With four drivers, I can hear so much more--and so many more flaws! I usually transfer music files into FLAC, and so I have pretty good sources for music. I've been using both my Samsung Galaxy S5 and Rockboxed iPod Video (equipped with a Fiio E11), and the sounds are great, but I'm noticing some files that weren't transferred correctly. I cannot connect to my computer speakers at work as the speakers do not have enough power to juice up the Quads, so be sure you have a more recent device or one with enough power to drive these IEMs.

I also use them on my Wii U's GamePad for Breath of the Wild, and they're actually better than my Audio-Technicas, even with the sliding ear tips. I hear a lot more, and sound is very important in the game.

All in all, amazing value for the price. The ear tip issue is more personal as my ears simply don't fit perfectly any of the ones provided, but I do wish the mic worked better.

I love this sound bar. Five stars for the audio. No doubt about it.
I consider myself relatively gadget-savvy, but certainly not tech-savvy. I love gadgets, but I'm an idiot when it comes to sound and sound-related technology. I only recently stopped using ear buds altogether and switched to my Sennheisers as my primary listening `phones.

My family and I live on the third floor of a three-apartment house, and not once did I ever consider getting surround sound. I have the speakers for it, as they were hand-me-downs, but I don't want to set them up lest I receive the wrath of my neighbors. That, and I don't even have the connections necessary on my TV (my TV is two years old; the speakers are far older than that). I recently heard about sound bars (though the PS3 one that came out a while ago caught my eye before), and thought that might be a better fit for me.

I don't normally track Vine orders, as they usually get delivered on Tuesdays. But I was so excited about this one I kept looking on UPS's website, only to be disappointed to read that it had not been delivered on Tuesday; when I got home, my hopes were ultimately crushed when I found the "undelivered" sticky on my mailbox. What's one more day? I signed the note and left it for the UPS man.
When I finally got the package the next day, I realized why they needed a signature: the box was huge! And there's no outer box, so all that's delivered is the product in its factory packaging, as if you bought it from the store yourself. Everybody and they momma are going to know what you ordered. But, thankfully, I don't have to worry about theft in my neighborhood too much.
So when I unboxed it, I was surprised to see how little real estate the actual sound bar took. Initially, I was surprised to see how big the box was, as I didn't think the bar itself was too big. But then I realized the box was oversized to accommodate the subwoofer.

Instructions were easy enough, but the HDMI set-up was a pain. There's a disc with the manual, but I would prefer if LG's website lets you download it (as of this review, they still don't have it up). Out of three HDMI cables I had lying around (two from the same brand), only one worked. I have two Mediabridge cables, one six- and the other nine-feet, and a cheapo one which came with my Comcast DVR. Only the Mediabridge six-foot cable worked, for some odd reason, so that's the one currently connecting the sound bar.
Nevertheless, the Internet capabilities are going to be wasted on me, I'm assuming, as I already have services such as Netflix on my PS3, and I don't see myself switching to the sound bar any time soon.
I haven't tried the other apps, so I can suggest getting this model without the Internet capabilities for the cheaper price tag. Really, you're paying $100-$150 just to have Wi-Fi on it, when many most likely have such services on other devices.

There's an optical cable included for the audio, as well as a wall mount. I won't use the mount till we buy a house, so I can't say much on that.

I love that the subwoofer is wireless. I knew where I wanted to place the sound bar and subwoofer before they arrived, and I was pleased that I was able to put them exactly where I wanted. I have a 47" Toshiba, so the sound bar and TV are perfectly matched.

My initial sound tests were Game of Thrones, Arrested Development, and Dexter's Laboratory (I'm a kid at heart), and the sound was amazing. I've never used other sound bars, but, considering this isn't a 5.1 surround sound system, I was blown away. The sound was perfect, exceeding my expectations. As I mentioned, I'm a newb to the audio world, so forgive my ignorance and bliss. I'm perfectly content with my sound bar, though, as our current "surround" sound system.

My wife didn't like it at first--and still kinda doesn't--as she thought "it's too loud," but over the first weekend, when we watched The Last Stand (awful movie, by the way), she changed her mind. She said it was like being in a theater--at least, the next best thing.

The bar itself is great, but the subwoofer really adds that punch where you can *feel* the sound. I have the subwoofer next to the couch for extra oomph.

All in all, I love it. I give the audio itself five stars, but I'm taking one star away for the Internet services. Honestly, I don't see the reason for paying the extra money when the other model with audio only is just as good. I still haven't used the video options, but will update this review if I ever do.

The remote is a bit large for just a sound bar, as I'm using only the power and volume buttons, as well as the occasional input button for Bluetooth. The latter feature is nice, but don't go moving your iPod/iPhone/other streaming device around, as the connection breaks easily. But when it's still, the music quality sounds great.

After getting this sound bar, I no longer care what my neighbors might think.

Best Wear OS for true Android users, but not perfect. I will avoid the facts that this watch is outdated at launch by its hardware (processor). That, coupled with retail and even discounted price also are out of step with the competition. These two big gripes aside. The watch is good and likely the best choice going into 2023 for pure Android Wear OS users (not looking at Apple or Tizen overlay users.)

Its not perfect and Pixel users will benefit the most when paired to this watch. Its lost most of the lag recent watches from other Wear OS brands. Has all the sensors the majority of buyers could want based on watch tech right now. It swipes, it plays well with the apps made for it. It gives you the info you ask of it. There are even a few nice 3rd part accessories now to avoid Google Gouging for proprietary bands. And there are few quirks I hope they iron out soon. Mainly, when the phone is in Bedtime Mode. Make the watch do it too, or add that Zen Mode feature to the watch also. It sucks to have animals tripping the security cameras outside dinging on my wrist and killing my sleep score. The snooze/do not disturb button on watch fails too easily and you have turn it on/off manually everytime.

As many claim, the battery sucks. Sort of. I can go up to 36+ hours on a slow day, and many others can too. It will depend on too many factors to list. But basically your popularity with notifications and thinking you need the screen always on are the biggest battery hurdles. Most can get use to touch to wake. And maybe only having text, phone, front door doorbell and one email be allowed to bother your watch with notifications. Do you really need to know what cousin Billy had at Dairy Queen when he posts the same pic/vid on Facebook, Instagram, Tic Toc and YouTube, etc. Find a nice balance of wrist information along with what sensors you need checking if you are still alive. You can start the day and track everything till the next morning when you charge it again while you shower and get the next day started. It charges quickly. And most other Wear OS watches have the same daily charge requirements. Nobody on Wear OS is winning on battery. Or Turn every setting all the way up and have a spare charger puck ready for a mid day juice. If you go that route. I suggest a quick release band to ease the removal of the watch.

So, its not up to the level or price of the Ultra Apple Watch. And if you don't care for Samsung. Your love for stock Android will eventually lead you back to this watch. Unless you forgo ECG sensors. The price will drop soon. Cases are minimizing the fragility of an ALL glass jelly bean design. But when comes to keeping your phone pocketed and yet still have info relayed in a useful way. Pixel Watch is the best current albeit not perfect solution for now.

Is This Really Necessary?. Notebook computers can overheat. It isn't a worry when you use your computer sparingly, but it can become a problem with extended usage. This cooling pad was designed to solve the problem by circulating air via two small fans with the power supplied by your notebook's USB. The movement of air is, supposedly, enough to keep your notebook from overheating or at least lessen the chances.

A product like this certainly sounds like a good idea and a practical solution to a problem, but does it really work as promised? Well, it does cause some extra flow of air, as expected, but the cooling effects are minimal. The main reason is because the flow of air is so light. Turn on the fans and place your hand next to them. You will barely feel anything and this is reason enough to suspect that it makes little difference.

Another thing to keep in mind with this cooling pad is that it will not work if you do not set it up properly. It has to be standing on a flat surface so that the air can flow underneath. If you're the type who holds your notebook on your lap, then a product like this will not work for you. There has to be space underneath so that the fans can operate and get the air moving.

The Mac Cooling Pad does fit securely on Mac's of different sizes and can be used for non- Mac pc's as well. I suppose it could make some difference in temperature, but it seems like a novelty product to me. Unless you are already experiencing an overheated notebook, a product like this is a waste of money.

Good Protective Cover and Stand for your Apple iPad2. The Targus VuScape Protective cover and stand is a pretty good, helpful aid for those who own an Apple Ipad2. It features a thin, lightweight design that is meant to hold the iPad2 snugly in place while you work.

Having a stand for your iPad is certainly a good idea and I like that this stand can be used to position your iPad in different ways. There are multiple grooves so that you can display your iPad at different angles. The cover can also be folded back completely, allowing the consumer to hold the iPad in the hands without the stand.

This protective cover/stand does have some nice features to offer, but after using it for a while, it is more than apparent that the stand is not perfect. Probably the greatest issue is that the stand isn't as sturdy as I would prefer. If you use the stand on a solid, flat surface, you shouldn't have too many problems, but place it on other surfaces and it tends to bend just a little bit. The slightest bend will cause the grooves to give way just a little, and the iPad will no longer be securely held in place.

I generally like the thin, lightweight design of this stand, but the thinness possibly goes a tad far. If the manufacturer had made this stand just a little bit thicker, it would be stronger and more likely to hold the iPad in place without any problems. I suppose this is the trade- off one must make when selecting a stand such as this. Lightweight is nice, especially for something like an iPad, but lightweight means the stand is lacking in strength.

All in all, this is a good stand and certainly worth considering, but not a deluxe stand like I expected. Again, as long as you are willing to sacrifice sturdiness for lightweight design, you should be fine. And try to use only on the flattest surfaces for the best results. Follow these guidelines and you should find yourself reasonably happy with this protective cover and stand from Targus.

Philips GoGear Vibe: Nothing Special, but Good for the Price. Philips GoGear Vibe 8 GB MP3 Player is a reasonably priced MP3 player from Philips Electronics. Small and with a good deal of memory, this MP3 player offers enough of the basic features to satisfy casual MP3 users' needs.

Let's talk about the good points first. This MP3 player is a good value and it has a long battery life. A full charge can last the better part of a day so it is ready when you need it. The compact size and durable construction are also plusses with this MP3 player. It takes up very little space and the metal construction is made to last. I like the menu navigation as well and found it very intuitive.

Most important to an MP3 player is sound quality and in this area, my feelings are mixed. My MP3 player experience is limited, so I have little to which I can compare. But based on other MP3 players, the sound quality with this Phillips device is a little below average. I was also very disappointed with the Full Sound option. This is supposed to improve the sound quality, but I could barely tell any difference. It has a little too much bass for my tastes, but others might find it acceptable.

Probably my greatest complaint with this Philips MP3 player is the included ear buds. They are the type that hugs the ear, but they do not contain a foam cushion and thus are not very comfortable or very good at blocking outside noise. The good thing, of course, is that an accessory like this can be replaced, which I recommend doing if you purchase this product.

MP3 players are nice and Philips GoGear Vibe 8 GB MP3 Player is a good MP3 player, especially for the price. There are certainly better MP3 players out there, but this is a good one for beginners or those with basic needs. I'm torn with my overall rating because of the division between the pros and cons. So, I will award this device with a middle rating of three stars and a modest recommendation.

Not Really Great. I was really looking forward to trying this tablet out. To date I'd had no exposure to Windows 8.1 or a dedicated Windows tablet. I have had a decent 10.1 inch Android tablet.

I have friends whose who online lives are conducted via five inch cell phone screens and they're happy with it. The screen on this tablet is nice. Don't get me wrong. I was able to stream from Amazon video in HD (720) and the video was crisp and clean. Images display well but, again, the screen is just seven inches. I can't imagine trying to be productive with something so small.

For a device with only one gig of RAM this runs Windows fairly well. I wws able to load several Windows programs including the Calibrě eBook manager which took a little longer to convert eBooks between formats but did the job. I also loaded a legacy email and Usenet program that I've been using for a decade or longer. Along with directly installed programs I also downloaded a handful of apps from the very buggy Microsoft app store. The store worked less than 50% of the time while I was trying this tablet out. I at one point had to resort to switching to a local login account and then back to my Hotmail logi. It only took about an hour of reading web forums to find that solution to the Windows app store refusing to work.

Two problems I ran into were the sound which is from a single speaker hidden in a slot on one of the short sides of the tablet. If you want to listen to anything other than the default Window's beeps and tones you'll want to pair this with a blue tooth speaker or headphones. The speaker in this tablet is deplorable. The next problem I had was the tablet runs HOT. I was running a program designed for Windows 98, downloading and reading posts un Usenet and viewing a few posted vacation and astronomy images and I had to stop. The tablet was so hot it was uncomfortable to hold and I worried it might overheat and become damaged.

While I was impressed to see Windows running on a small tablet I was thoroughly unimpressed with Windows 8.1 the tile system is just terrible.

So, it has good video quality on a too small screen with horrible sound and a flaky app store to rely upon, though you can download and install normal Windows programs. I just wasn't that crazy about this tablet. And will definitely be sticking with Android and a much larger screen.

And that there's where the plus side ends...

I shot over 850 images meticulously testing settings and options in numerous situations and ended up with three pictures I thought were really good.

The low light capability even at 20mm wide angle was sub-par. One of my favorite activities is to sit at the beaches here in Florida and watch the sunrise. I've always got a camera with me. Images pre-dawn and at sunrise were... grainy, cluttered, blurry.

Post dawn, full light shots of surfers looked like Pointilization art. Even when only zooming out 20x - 30x, far from the extreme limit of the camera, I didn't get one picture I bothered to keep out of well over 150 tries.

I also went to a horse show. Full daylight, light fluffy clouds and again shooting well below the full 60x (1,200mm) zoom of the camera and the results were horrid, grainy, full of noise. Many shots looked like badly done art filters in Photoshop rather than photographs from a moderately expensive bridge camera. I also shot a few images at the horse show under the shade of trees and even in iA mode letting the camera pick all the settings and not zooming in at all, images were dark, mottled and grainy.

In conclusion... I have an older 30x camera that's getting on in age. I had hoped to retire it and replace it with a new more modern camera. I just wasn't impressed enough with the Panasonic Lumix FZ70. The functionality was great but that's not the most important aspect of a camera, photo quality is and I just wasn't happy enough with the results and returned the camera. A seller replaced a different defective FM transmitter unit with this one for me (mine has the Kollea brand name on it, but this is the identical unit, private-labeled). This is a better product than what it replaced, but is not without it's flaws. I have three (*UPDATE: now four, and the fourth one is a deal-breaker--see below) complaints with this unit:

1) It will not automatically reconnect to my phone about 75% of the time. I have to manually shut Bluetooth off and turn it back on on the phone, sometimes a few times before it pairs successfully. This is a hassle--a PITA. Every time I get in the car, I have to go through this process--every time power is cut from the transmitter, actually, so if your passenger knocks it and it pops out of the 12V socket, it will have to be re-paired, which is supposed to happen automatically, but does not, and you then have to go through the process. Frustrating.

2) Charge output is only 1.0A. this is why I returned the first one--phone gives a "slow charging" warning when charging from this unit, regardless of what USB cable I use (I tried four different cables, all of which I know for certain can carry 2.1A).

3) Callers have occasionally complained they cannot hear me well when using this unit, and I occasionally (but not often) encounter FM interference. I believe Bluetooth itself is part of the problem, and anyone who has used a few Bluetooth headsets or units like this knows audio quality is terrible. Period. We just deal with it. Add to that the burden of having to transmit your signal via FM to a car stereo and the user-side audio (what you will hear in your car) is always going to be craptastic.

4) (*UPDATE) When paired, voice recognition on my phone, which is usually quite good, becomes severely impaired. This is also likely the culprit for complaint #3, above. I suspect this is because when paired, it tries to use the built-in microphone for voice recognition instead of the microphones on my phone (of which there are 4). It is disabling the extremely good microphones in my phone (Nokia lumia Icon which is well known for having incredible audio input) and using the unit's crappy microphone instead. This microphone is located in the unit, which is attached to the center console of my car near the shifter, and thus picks up all the vibrations and related road and engine noise transmitted through the structure of the car as I drive. This approach is terrible. I have stopped using the unit for anything requiring voice input, including telephone calls. In other words, this is just a big awkward charger now, and one that charges painfully slowly (see complaint #2). If it were possible to disable the onboard mic, and use the mics in my phone instead for calls and voice recognition, this would be a much more serviceable unit As it is now, it is just a piece of junk.

Interesting, but not terribly practical and could be improved. Up front I received this as a review sample and as much as I would love to love it, I just do not. Here are a few reasons why, which I will get out of the way first so I can end this review on a more positive note. However, first I am going to try to describe what this is: an Android tablet in a camera form factor.

Foremost among the reasons why I subtracted stars is the instructions do not begin to scratch the surface. Even the quick start instructions did not disclose any illustration details of the buttons and ports. In fact, there were no details about inserting the paper for prints or even specs like charging times and how much use you can expect on a full charge. For an experienced Android phone and tablet user some of the missing information is a mere inconvenience. For someone accustomed to IOS or other types of phones and tablets the learning curve can be daunting.

Second, since this is a full blown tablet the screen should have been larger in relation to the overall form factor. Instead the printing mechanism takes up real estate that would be better suited to allocating to the screen. Indeed, the mere fact that this has a printer at all is a head scratcher for me because the near seamless connectivity to remote printing that this device's software allows obviates the need for on the spot printing. In this day and age photos are mainly shared in digital form with only occasional need for hard copies. Especially when thirty prints from a pack of Zero-Ink paper runs about fifteen bucks at the time of this review - see [[ASIN:B008GVVTPU Polaroid 2x3" Premium ZINK Zero Ink Paper 30-Pack]].

Since this is camera-centric the lack of a 1/4-20 threaded mount for tripods is a glaring omission and yet another reason why I subtracted two stars.

THE GOOD: this is a full fledged Android computer that is a breeze to set up and configure. I had that part up and operational in less than five minutes. Do bear in mind that not only am I a retired IT professional, but have extensive Android experience, so for folks like myself the dearth of documentation is not an issue. Even a novice user can follow the basic set-up instructions, which allow you to skip steps and come back later.

Although the screen is not as large as I would have liked, it is more than sufficient for most tasks and is a lot larger than my Galaxy Note 3 phone's screen.

The computing part is relatively fast too. I was able to browse web sites at brisk speeds, and uploading photos to facebook was as fast as from my Note 3 phone or my Samsung Tab 3 10.1 tablet - both of which are fairly quick.

Bottom line for me: unless you absolutely need the ability to print 3x2 inch photos you would probably be better off with a small tablet, which makes more sense and does everything else that this camera does (except the hard copy prints.) Of course, if you need hard copy prints and 3x2 inch ones are adequate, this may be just what you need.
